SECTIONS.title: The study of life
ideas: Living things share properties: order, evolutionary adaptation, response to the environment, regulation (homeostasis), energy processing, growth and development, and reproduction.

Biology is organized in levels: molecules → organelles → cells → tissues → organs → organisms → populations → communities → ecosystems → the biosphere. Emergent properties appear at each level from the arrangement and interactions of parts.

Five unifying themes: organization (structure fits function), information (DNA → RNA → protein), energy and matter (energy flows through ecosystems, matter cycles), interactions (feedback regulation) and, the core theme, evolution.
Life is classified into three domains: Bacteria and Archaea (prokaryotes) and Eukarya (protists, plants, fungi, animals). Darwin’s natural selection explains both the unity and the diversity of life.

Science tests hypotheses: explanations that must be testable and falsifiable. A controlled experiment changes one independent variable, measures a dependent variable and compares against a control group. A theory is broad and backed by a large body of evidence.

SECTIONS.title: The chemical context of life
ideas: About 96% of living matter is C, H, O and N. An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons in shells; the atomic number is the number of protons and the mass number is protons + neutrons.
Isotopes have the same number of protons but different neutrons. Radioactive isotopes decay at a fixed half-life (carbon-14 about 5,730 years) and are used as tracers and for dating.
Chemical behavior depends on valence electrons in the outer shell. Atoms form bonds to fill it: H makes 1 bond, O 2, N 3, C 4.

Covalent bonds share electrons: nonpolar when shared equally, polar when one atom is more electronegative (O and N pull hard). Ionic bonds form between ions with opposite charges after an electron is transferred (Na⁺Cl⁻).

Weak bonds shape biology: hydrogen bonds (a partially positive H attracted to an electronegative O or N), van der Waals interactions and ionic attractions in water. Molecular shape determines function, as with enzymes, receptors and drugs.

SECTIONS.title: Water and life
ideas: Water is polar: oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive charges, so each molecule can hydrogen-bond with up to four neighbors.
Hydrogen bonding explains cohesion (water sticks to itself, giving surface tension and helping water move up plants) and adhesion (water sticks to other surfaces).

Water moderates temperature: high specific heat (1 cal/g·°C) and high heat of vaporization give evaporative cooling. Ice floats because its hydrogen bonds hold molecules farther apart, so it is less dense than liquid water.
Water is a versatile solvent for ions and polar molecules (hydrophilic); nonpolar molecules are hydrophobic. Concentration is measured in molarity (moles per liter).

pH = −log[H⁺]. Each unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]; pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic, and [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴. Buffers resist pH changes (the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer in blood). Rising CO₂ makes oceans more acidic.

SECTIONS.title: Carbon and the molecular diversity of life
ideas: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, so it forms 4 covalent bonds, building chains, branches, rings and double bonds: the skeletons of organic molecules.

Isomers have the same formula but different structures: structural isomers (different arrangement of atoms), cis-trans isomers (different arrangement around a double bond) and enantiomers (mirror images; often only one form is active, as with some drugs).

Seven chemical groups to know: hydroxyl (–OH, polar, alcohols), carbonyl (C=O, ketones and aldehydes), carboxyl (–COOH, acidic), amino (–NH₂, basic), sulfhydryl (–SH, forms disulfide bridges), phosphate (–OPO₃²⁻, stores energy in ATP) and methyl (–CH₃, affects gene expression).
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is an organic molecule whose phosphate groups release energy when one is removed.
Hydrocarbons (only C and H) are nonpolar and hydrophobic; adding polar groups such as –OH makes molecules more soluble in water.

SECTIONS.title: Carbohydrates and lipids
ideas: Polymers are built by dehydration synthesis (removing a water molecule for each bond) and broken by hydrolysis (adding water).

Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) join by glycosidic linkages into disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose) and polysaccharides.

Storage polysaccharides: starch in plants and glycogen (highly branched) in animals, both α-glucose. Structural: cellulose (β-glucose, which most animals cannot digest) in plant cell walls and chitin in arthropod exoskeletons and fungal walls.

Fats (triglycerides) are glycerol plus three fatty acids joined by ester linkages. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds and pack tightly (solid at room temperature); unsaturated ones have cis double bonds that kink the chain (liquid oils). Trans fats are harmful.

Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic tails, so they form bilayers. Steroids have four fused rings; cholesterol sits in animal membranes and is the starting point for sex hormones. Lipids are not true polymers.

SECTIONS.title: Proteins: structure and function
ideas: Proteins do most of the cell’s work: enzymes, structure, transport, storage, hormones, receptors, movement and defense.

An amino acid has a central carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group. The 20 amino acids are grouped by R group: nonpolar (hydrophobic), polar and electrically charged (acidic or basic).
Amino acids join by peptide bonds (dehydration synthesis) into a polypeptide with an N-terminus and a C-terminus.

Four levels of structure: primary (the amino acid sequence), secondary (α helices and β pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms), tertiary (the 3-D shape from R-group interactions: hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and covalent disulfide bridges) and quaternary (two or more polypeptides, such as hemoglobin).

Shape determines function. A single amino acid change can matter: in sickle-cell disease, valine replaces glutamic acid in hemoglobin. Heat, pH or salt can denature a protein by disrupting its shape; chaperonins help proteins fold.

SECTIONS.title: Nucleic acids
ideas: DNA stores hereditary information; RNA carries it out (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA). Genes are DNA sequences that direct protein synthesis through mRNA.
A nucleotide = a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) + a nitrogenous base + one or more phosphate groups.
Purines (adenine, guanine) have two rings; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one. DNA uses T; RNA uses U instead.
Nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester linkages into a sugar-phosphate backbone with a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (hydroxyl).

DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). RNA is usually single-stranded but can fold on itself.

SECTIONS.title: Metabolism and energy
ideas: Metabolism is all of an organism’s chemical reactions. Catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy (cellular respiration); anabolic pathways build molecules and consume energy (protein synthesis).
Kinetic energy is energy of motion (heat is the kinetic energy of molecules); potential energy is stored by position or structure, including chemical energy in bonds.

The first law of thermodynamics: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred or transformed. The second law: every energy transfer increases the entropy (disorder) of the universe, and some energy is lost as heat.
Free energy ΔG = ΔH − TΔS predicts whether a reaction is spontaneous. Exergonic reactions release free energy (ΔG < 0, spontaneous); endergonic reactions absorb it (ΔG > 0, not spontaneous).
Cells are open systems that never reach equilibrium; a cell at equilibrium is dead. Metabolic pathways keep reactions moving by removing products.

SECTIONS.title: ATP and enzymes
ideas: ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pᵢ releases about −7.3 kcal/mol under standard conditions. Cells use energy coupling: the phosphate is transferred to another molecule (phosphorylation), making it more reactive. ATP is regenerated from ADP by respiration.
Enzymes are catalysts (usually proteins) that speed reactions by lowering the activation energy. They do not change ΔG or the equilibrium, and they are not used up.

The substrate binds the active site; the fit tightens as the enzyme changes shape (induced fit). Enzymes are specific and have optimal temperature and pH; many need cofactors (metal ions) or coenzymes (organic, often vitamins).

Competitive inhibitors bind the active site (overcome by more substrate); noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the enzyme’s shape. Allosteric regulation turns enzymes on or off at a separate site.
Feedback inhibition: the end product of a pathway inhibits an early enzyme, so the cell does not overproduce it.

SECTIONS.title: Cellular respiration
ideas: Overall: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP and heat). It is a series of redox reactions: glucose is oxidized and O₂ is reduced. Electrons travel on the carriers NAD⁺ → NADH and FAD → FADH₂.
Glycolysis (cytosol, no O₂ needed): glucose → 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix): each pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH. The citric acid cycle (matrix), per glucose (two turns): 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 4 CO₂.

Oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane): the electron transport chain passes electrons to O₂, the final electron acceptor, forming water, while pumping H⁺ into the intermembrane space. H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), making most of the ATP: about 30–32 ATP per glucose in total.

Without O₂, fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue: alcohol fermentation (pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂, in yeast) or lactic acid fermentation (in muscle). Fermentation yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

SECTIONS.title: A tour of the cell
ideas: All cells have a plasma membrane, cytosol, chromosomes and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, with DNA in a nucleoid; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and organelles.
Cells stay small because the surface-area-to-volume ratio falls as size grows; a large cell cannot exchange materials fast enough.

The endomembrane system: the nuclear envelope, the rough ER (ribosomes, makes secreted and membrane proteins), the smooth ER (lipids, detoxification, calcium storage), the Golgi apparatus (modifies, sorts and ships), lysosomes (digestive enzymes) and vacuoles (the plant central vacuole).

Mitochondria (respiration) and chloroplasts (photosynthesis) have their own DNA, ribosomes and double membranes, supporting the endosymbiont theory. Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins, producing H₂O₂.

The cytoskeleton: microtubules (tubulin; cilia, flagella, spindle), microfilaments (actin; muscle, cell shape, cleavage furrow) and intermediate filaments (tension). Outside: plant cell walls, the animal extracellular matrix, and junctions (plasmodesmata, tight junctions, desmosomes, gap junctions).

SECTIONS.title: Membrane structure and transport
ideas: The fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that drift laterally. Unsaturated tails keep it fluid; cholesterol buffers fluidity against temperature changes.
Membrane proteins are integral (span the bilayer) or peripheral; they transport, act as enzymes and receptors, and help cells recognize and attach to each other (glycoproteins).
Selective permeability: small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) cross freely; ions and polar molecules need transport proteins: channels (including aquaporins for water) and carriers.

Passive transport goes down a concentration gradient with no energy: diffusion, osmosis (water) and facilitated diffusion. Tonicity: in a hypotonic solution water enters (animal cells may burst; plant cells become turgid), in a hypertonic one water leaves (animal cells shrivel; plant cells plasmolyze), and isotonic means no net movement.

Active transport uses energy to move solutes against their gradient: the sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, building the membrane potential; cotransport uses one gradient to drive another. Bulk transport: exocytosis and endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated).

SECTIONS.title: The cell cycle and mitosis
ideas: A duplicated chromosome is two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Human body cells are diploid: 2n = 46.
The cell cycle: interphase (G₁ growth, S DNA replication, G₂ preparation) and the mitotic phase (mitosis + cytokinesis). Prokaryotes divide by binary fission.

Mitosis: prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), prometaphase (nuclear envelope breaks down, kinetochore microtubules attach), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to opposite poles) and telophase (nuclei re-form).
Cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow pinches animal cells (an actin ring); plant cells build a cell plate from Golgi vesicles.

Control: checkpoints at G₁ (the main “restriction point”), G₂ and M (all chromosomes attached to the spindle before anaphase). Cyclins bind Cdks (such as MPF) to drive the cycle; growth factors, density-dependent inhibition and anchorage dependence add signals. Cancer cells ignore these controls.

SECTIONS.title: Meiosis and life cycles
ideas: Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes (one from each parent). Diploid (2n) cells have two sets; haploid (n) gametes have one. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus the sex chromosomes.

Meiosis I separates homologs (reduces 2n to n): in prophase I homologs pair (synapsis) and exchange segments by crossing over at chiasmata; in anaphase I homologs move apart while sister chromatids stay together. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis. One cell becomes four genetically different haploid cells.

Life cycles: animals make gametes by meiosis; plants and some algae show alternation of generations, with a multicellular diploid sporophyte making haploid spores by meiosis, which grow into a multicellular haploid gametophyte that makes gametes by mitosis; fungi and many protists have a haploid adult and a diploid zygote only.

Three sources of genetic variation (the “meiotic superpowers”): independent assortment of homologs (2ⁿ combinations; 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million in humans), crossing over, and random fertilization (about 70 trillion zygote combinations before crossing over).
Errors: nondisjunction (homologs or sisters fail to separate) produces aneuploid gametes, as in trisomy 21.

SECTIONS.title: Mendel and the gene idea
ideas: Mendel crossed true-breeding pea plants (P generation) to get the F₁, then self-crossed them to get the F₂. Alleles are versions of a gene; a dominant allele masks a recessive one.
Genotype is the allele combination (homozygous AA or aa, heterozygous Aa); phenotype is the trait. A testcross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype.
Law of segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes. A monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio and 1:2:1 genotypes.

Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes sort independently. A dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb gives 9:3:3:1. Use the multiplication rule for “and” (independent events) and the addition rule for “or” (mutually exclusive outcomes).

Beyond Mendel: incomplete dominance (1:2:1 phenotypes, pink snapdragons), codominance (both expressed, AB blood), multiple alleles (ABO), pleiotropy (one gene, many effects), epistasis (one gene masks another, 9:3:4) and polygenic traits (height). Pedigrees trace traits such as cystic fibrosis (recessive) and Huntington’s disease (dominant).

SECTIONS.title: Linked genes and linkage mapping
ideas: The chromosome theory of inheritance: genes sit on chromosomes, and chromosome behavior in meiosis explains Mendel’s laws. Thomas Hunt Morgan’s fruit flies showed an eye-color gene on the X chromosome.

Sex-linked (X-linked) recessive traits, such as red-green color blindness, hemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, appear far more often in males, who have one X. In female mammals one X is inactivated as a Barr body.

Linked genes sit close together on one chromosome and tend to be inherited together, so they do not assort independently. Crossing over produces recombinant offspring with new combinations; the rest are parental types.
Recombination frequency = recombinants ÷ total offspring × 100. It tracks distance: 1% = 1 map unit (centimorgan). It never exceeds 50%, which looks the same as independent assortment.

A linkage map orders genes using the pairwise distances (the two genes farthest apart are at the ends). Chromosome changes include deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations; nondisjunction causes aneuploidy (trisomy 21, XXY, XO).

SECTIONS.title: Odds and ends: genes in populations
ideas: A population’s gene pool is all its alleles. Microevolution is a change in allele frequencies over generations.
The Hardy–Weinberg equation describes a population that is not evolving: allele frequencies p + q = 1 and genotype frequencies p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (AA, Aa, aa).

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium assumes no mutations, random mating, no natural selection, a very large population (no genetic drift) and no gene flow. Real populations violate these, which is how evolution happens.
To solve problems, start from the homozygous recessive frequency: q² = fraction showing the recessive trait, so q = √(q²), p = 1 − q, and carriers = 2pq.
Genetic variation comes from mutation and sexual reproduction; natural selection, genetic drift (founder and bottleneck effects) and gene flow change allele frequencies.

SECTIONS.title: DNA: the genetic material and its structure
ideas: Griffith (1928): harmless bacteria were transformed by heat-killed virulent bacteria. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identified the transforming substance as DNA.
Hershey and Chase (1952) labeled phage DNA with ³²P and protein with ³⁵S; only the ³²P entered the bacteria, showing that DNA is the genetic material.
Chargaff’s rules: base composition varies between species, and in DNA %A = %T and %G = %C.

Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray images showed a helix; Watson and Crick built the double-helix model: two antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones outside, paired bases inside, about 2 nm wide, with a full turn every 3.4 nm (10 base pairs).
A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine (A–T, G–C), keeping the width uniform. The sequence of bases carries the information.

SECTIONS.title: DNA replication
ideas: Replication is semiconservative: each new double helix has one old and one new strand (shown by Meselson and Stahl with ¹⁵N and ¹⁴N).
At each origin, helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins hold the strands apart and topoisomerase relieves twisting ahead of the fork. Primase lays down a short RNA primer.
DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in Okazaki fragments.
DNA polymerase I replaces RNA primers with DNA, and DNA ligase joins the fragments.

DNA polymerases proofread; mismatch repair and nucleotide excision repair fix errors that remain. Linear chromosomes shorten at their ends each round; telomerase extends telomeres in germ cells and many cancer cells.

SECTIONS.title: Gene expression: transcription and RNA processing
ideas: The central dogma: DNA → RNA (transcription) → protein (translation). In eukaryotes transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm.

RNA polymerase binds a promoter (in eukaryotes with the help of transcription factors, often at a TATA box), unwinds DNA and builds RNA 5′ → 3′ by reading the template strand 3′ → 5′. No primer is needed.
The mRNA matches the coding (non-template) strand except that U replaces T.
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed: a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail are added (protection and export), and introns are removed while exons are joined by the spliceosome.
Alternative splicing lets one gene produce several different proteins.

SECTIONS.title: Translation and mutations
ideas: The genetic code reads mRNA in codons of three bases: 64 codons, 61 for amino acids and 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). AUG codes for methionine and is the start codon. The code is redundant and nearly universal.
tRNA carries an amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a codon. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acid to each tRNA.
The ribosome (rRNA + protein) has three sites: A (the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA), P (holds the growing polypeptide) and E (exit). The rRNA catalyzes peptide bonds.

Stages: initiation (small subunit, mRNA and initiator tRNA at AUG, then the large subunit), elongation (codon recognition, peptide bond, translocation) and termination (a release factor at a stop codon). Many ribosomes can translate one mRNA (polyribosomes).

Point mutations: silent (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid, as in sickle-cell disease) and nonsense (an early stop codon). Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshifts.

SECTIONS.title: DNA technology
ideas: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences (EcoRI cuts GAATTC), often leaving sticky ends. Fragments with matching ends are joined by DNA ligase to make recombinant DNA.
Gene cloning: insert a gene into a plasmid vector, transform bacteria, select with an antibiotic-resistance gene, and let the bacteria copy it.
Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move farther.
PCR copies a target sequence: denature at about 95 °C, anneal primers at about 50–65 °C, extend with heat-stable Taq polymerase at about 72 °C. Each cycle doubles the copies: 2ⁿ after n cycles.

Sanger sequencing uses dideoxynucleotides that stop synthesis; next-generation methods sequence millions of fragments at once. CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to lead the Cas9 nuclease to a target sequence, where it cuts both strands so the gene can be disrupted or edited.
